doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

chapter: Hearing the bands and the rhythm guitar ideal
title: Rhythm section feel; how he came to sing and solo
summary: A friend takes a big band course; as groups shrank he began soloing and singing in Chicago, though he still prefers the rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: jogging or lifting weights or something like similar to that, you know, you have to use a higher action and heavier gauge strings. But once you get it going, you know, he said, “It’s a wonderful feeling. I was with the bass and the drums and we were all tight, together and we got a blend” and stuff like that. So but getting back to your question, so that’s what I really wanted to do. And it was, if I did take some crappy solos once in a while, that came later. That came because as the music business got worse and worse, I mean less and less employment and groups got smaller and smaller, they wanted somebody who could do something. Hence, I also started to do the vocals. I remember I was in Chicago about 1954, ‘55 or something like that. Some guys, we were always sitting around the back room during the intermissions you know, and I’d be singing little songs and playing. He says, “Do that on stage.” He says, “We need all the help we can get.” And I said, oh, you know, I was like totally inhibited about it. So I got up and sort of mumbled and didn’t look at the audience and everything, the way you do, but it’s like public speaking or something. Gradually they shove you out there enough times and you know you get used to it. That’s how that came about. But basically my favorite thing still is to just play in the rhythm section. If they don’t give me a solo all night I don’t give a damn. You know I don’t really care.
That feeling that a good rhythm section with a piano, guitar and bass and drums, it’s hard to define when it’s really happening. But as you said, it’s a special feeling.
